reconcile.connective: Reformed commentators take the choice-commands as real summonses whose root is God's prior election, so the call to “choose” and the doctrine of predestination describe one work, not two rival ones.

discrepancy.connective: Voltaire pressed the sharpest objection, ridiculing the predestinarian doctrine of grace as irreconcilable with the moral liberty Scripture itself demands when it bids people choose.

excerpts.excerpt_text: That is, love and obey God: which thing is not in man’s power, but God’s Spirit only worketh it in his elect.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly subordinates the “choose life” command to election: the very obedience commanded is wrought by God in the elect, harmonizing the choice text with the predestination texts.

excerpts.excerpt_text: he here puts them to their choice, not as if it were antecedently indifferent whether they served God or nor, or as if they were at liberty to refuse his service …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Reads Joshua's “choose you this day” as a genuine summons that nonetheless does not make humans free to refuse God's service, reconciling the choice-command with divine sovereignty.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Joshua 24:15
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this passage directly, arguing the call to choose is God's revealed will yet leaves no real liberty to refuse him — a harmonizing reading of the choice/sovereignty tension keyed to this verse.
